notes.front: What is hyperventilation?
notes.back: An excessive rate and depth of breathing that causes an abnormal loss of carbon dioxide from the blood.
notes.explanation: It often starts in a stressful moment; it rarely incapacitates, but its symptoms can alarm and distract a pilot.
notes.example: A pilot startled by a near miss starts breathing fast and feels dizzy and tingly.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 45

notes.front: What is stress, physiologically?
notes.back: The body’s response to physical and psychological demands placed on it.
notes.explanation: Stress raises heart rate, breathing and blood pressure, and too much of it degrades performance and decisions.
notes.example: Noise and vibration (physical), fatigue (physiological) and personal problems (psychological) are all stressors.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 46

notes.front: What is acute stress?
notes.back: Short-term stress from an immediate threat perceived as danger, triggering the “fight or flight” response.
notes.explanation: A healthy person normally copes with it, but ongoing acute stress can become chronic stress.
notes.example: The jolt you feel when a gust suddenly pushes the aircraft towards a tree.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 46

notes.front: What is chronic stress?
notes.back: Long-term stress that becomes an intolerable burden, exceeds the ability to cope, and makes performance fall sharply.
notes.explanation: Pilots at this level are not safe to fly and should see a doctor.
notes.example: Months of money worries and relationship problems building up.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 46

notes.front: What is fatigue, and why does it matter to a pilot?
notes.back: Physical or mental tiredness; it degrades attention, concentration, coordination and communication.
notes.explanation: It is frequently associated with pilot error and seriously affects decision-making.
notes.example: After a 14-hour working day your reactions and judgement are slower, even if you feel fine.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 46

notes.front: What is acute fatigue?
notes.back: Short-term tiredness after strenuous effort, excitement or lack of sleep, normally cured by rest and 8 hours of sound sleep.
notes.explanation: A remote pilot with acute fatigue should not operate a small UA.
notes.example: Feeling worn out after a long hot day of site surveys.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 46

notes.front: What is chronic fatigue?
notes.back: Long-lasting fatigue, usually with psychological roots, that rest and diet do not relieve.
notes.explanation: It usually needs treatment by a physician.
notes.example: Weeks of weakness, headaches and irritability that a weekend off does not fix.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 47

notes.front: What is skill fatigue?
notes.back: A special type of acute fatigue that disrupts timing and narrows the perceptual field.
notes.explanation: The pilot seems to perform normally, but control movements lose smoothness and accuracy.
notes.example: Stick inputs becoming jerky and focused only on the centre of the screen late in a long session.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 46

notes.front: What is dehydration?
notes.back: A critical loss of water from the body.
notes.explanation: Its first noticeable effect is fatigue, which makes top physical and mental performance hard or impossible.
notes.example: Standing in summer sun all afternoon with only coffee to drink.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 47

notes.front: What is heatstroke?
notes.back: A condition caused by any inability of the body to control its temperature.
notes.explanation: It may show first as dehydration symptoms, or only as a sudden collapse.
notes.example: A pilot working all day on a hot, shadeless site who suddenly collapses.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 48

notes.front: What is a visual scan, as taught to pilots?
notes.back: A systematic search of the sky in a series of short, regularly spaced eye stops across the field of view.
notes.explanation: A disciplined pattern of stops makes sure the whole area is searched for traffic.
notes.example: Looking left to right in blocks about 30° wide, pausing on each.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 50

notes.front: What are rods and cones in the eye?
notes.back: Light-sensitive cells: cones give colour and fine detail in good light; rods see in dim light but not colour.
notes.explanation: At night the rods do most of the work, which changes how you must look at things.
notes.example: At dusk colours fade to grey because the cones are losing sensitivity.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Vision in Flight”, p. 17-20

notes.front: What is the night blind spot?
notes.back: A blind area at the centre of the field of view at night, where cones are concentrated and rods are few.
notes.explanation: An object looked at directly at night can disappear, so pilots look slightly off centre.
notes.example: A dim light that vanishes when you stare straight at it.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Night Blind Spot”, p. 17-22

notes.front: What is dark adaptation?
notes.back: The eye’s adjustment to a dark environment, mostly by the rods.
notes.explanation: Until it is complete, night vision is weaker, and a bright light can undo it.
notes.example: Walking from bright sunlight into a dark cinema.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Dark Adaptation”, p. 17-23

notes.front: What is autokinesis?
notes.back: A night illusion in which a stationary light, stared at for a few seconds against a dark background, appears to move.
notes.explanation: A remote pilot staring at their aircraft’s light at night may misjudge its movement.
notes.example: A single light on a mast seems to drift after you stare at it.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Autokinesis”, p. 17-26

notes.front: What is a false horizon?
notes.back: An illusion in which features such as sloping clouds or patterns of ground lights and stars are mistaken for the real horizon.
notes.explanation: It can make a pilot misjudge attitude, especially at night.
notes.example: Shoreline lights at night mistaken for stars in the sky.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “False Horizon”, p. 17-26

notes.front: What is self-imposed stress, as it affects night vision?
notes.back: Stress a pilot causes and can control, such as drugs, exhaustion, poor fitness, alcohol, tobacco and missed meals.
notes.explanation: These factors can limit night vision, and knowing them lets pilots avoid them.
notes.example: Smoking and skipping dinner before a night job.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Self-Imposed Stress”, p. 17-25

notes.front: Whose responsibility is it that no crew member takes part in an operation while impaired?
notes.back: The remote PIC’s.
notes.explanation: This covers the person manipulating the controls and the visual observer as well as the remote PIC.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 45

notes.front: Which medical condition does the study guide give as an example that may create a risk to operations?
notes.back: Epilepsy; the remote PIC must decide whether the condition is under control and they can fly safely.
notes.explanation: Certain medical conditions, like certain medications, can affect safe operation.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 45

notes.front: The study guide’s list of medical factors pilots should know covers hyperventilation, stress, fatigue, dehydration, the effects of alcohol and drugs, and {{c1::heatstroke}}.
notes.explanation: Each gets its own section in the study guide’s physiology chapter.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 45

notes.front: Which common over-the-counter drugs can cause drowsiness and cognitive deficits?
notes.back: Antihistamines and decongestants.
notes.explanation: Treating a cold with them can compound the problem the cold already causes.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 48

notes.front: Why is diphenhydramine (e.g. Benadryl) singled out?
notes.back: It causes drowsiness and has a long half-life, so side effects last a long time.
notes.explanation: A drug that stays in the system extends the period you should not fly.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 49

notes.front: After the first dose of any new medication, prescription or over-the-counter, how long should you wait before flying?
notes.back: At least 48 hours.
notes.explanation: The wait shows whether you have side effects that would make it unsafe to operate.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 49

notes.front: Besides alcohol, what drug use do part 107 and §§91.17 and 91.19 prohibit?
notes.back: Using any drug that affects the person’s faculties in any way contrary to safety.
notes.explanation: There is no list of banned medicines; the test is the effect on safety.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 48

notes.front: How long can considerable amounts of alcohol remain in the body?
notes.back: Over 16 hours.
notes.explanation: So be cautious about flying too soon after drinking, even after the 8-hour rule is met.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 49

notes.front: Is a pilot with a hangover still under the influence of alcohol?
notes.back: Yes; motor and mental impairment is still present, even if the pilot feels normal.
notes.explanation: The study guide advises being more conservative than the regulations.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 49

notes.front: How much alcohol can reduce the speed and strength of muscular reflexes?
notes.back: As little as one ounce.
notes.explanation: Impairments in vision and hearing can come from as little as one drink.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 49

notes.front: Eight hours after drinking, a pilot’s blood alcohol is still 0.04 percent. May they fly?
notes.back: No; they must wait until it falls below 0.04 percent.
notes.explanation: Both limits apply: at least 8 hours since drinking, and below 0.04 percent.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 50

notes.front: The study guide’s common symptoms of hyperventilation are {{c1::visual impairment}}, unconsciousness, a lightheaded or dizzy feeling, tingling, hot and cold sensations and muscle spasms.
notes.explanation: The symptoms can alarm an uninformed pilot, and the resulting anxiety makes breathing faster still.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 45

notes.explanation: The symptoms can alarm an uninformed pilot, and the resulting anxiety makes breathing faster still.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 45

notes.explanation: The symptoms can alarm an uninformed pilot, and the resulting anxiety makes breathing faster still.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 45

notes.front: The study guide’s common symptoms of hyperventilation are visual impairment, unconsciousness, a lightheaded or dizzy feeling, {{c1::tingling}}, hot and cold sensations and muscle spasms.
notes.explanation: The symptoms can alarm an uninformed pilot, and the resulting anxiety makes breathing faster still.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 45

notes.front: The study guide’s common symptoms of hyperventilation are visual impairment, unconsciousness, a lightheaded or dizzy feeling, tingling, {{c1::hot and cold sensations}} and muscle spasms.
notes.explanation: The symptoms can alarm an uninformed pilot, and the resulting anxiety makes breathing faster still.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 45

notes.front: The study guide’s common symptoms of hyperventilation are visual impairment, unconsciousness, a lightheaded or dizzy feeling, tingling, hot and cold sensations and {{c1::muscle spasms}}.
notes.explanation: The symptoms can alarm an uninformed pilot, and the resulting anxiety makes breathing faster still.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 45

notes.front: What three things help overcome hyperventilation?
notes.back: Slowing the breathing rate, breathing into a paper bag, and talking aloud.
notes.explanation: Treatment restores the carbon dioxide level; recovery is usually rapid once breathing is normal.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 46

notes.front: What commonly triggers hyperventilation in pilots?
notes.back: An unexpected stressful situation, which may make them subconsciously breathe faster.
notes.explanation: Anxiety then aggravates it, so knowing the symptoms helps break the cycle.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 45

notes.front: What is an example of each type of stressor: physical, physiological and psychological?
notes.back: Physical: noise or vibration. Physiological: fatigue. Psychological: difficult work or personal situations.
notes.explanation: A stressor is anything that causes an individual to experience stress.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 46

notes.front: What should a pilot who suspects chronic stress do?
notes.back: Stop flying and see a doctor.
notes.explanation: At chronic stress levels performance falls off rapidly.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 46

notes.front: Which two techniques does the study guide give for managing stress?
notes.back: Setting aside time each day to relax or keeping fit, and managing time well to avoid deadline pressure.
notes.explanation: A certain amount of stress keeps a pilot alert; too much becomes an intolerable burden.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 10, p. 62

notes.front: What ordinarily cures acute fatigue?
notes.back: Rest after exertion and 8 hours of sound sleep.
notes.explanation: Proper diet and adequate rest and sleep also prevent it.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 46

notes.front: Can training or experience overcome fatigue that sets in during a small UA operation?
notes.back: No; adequate rest is the only way to prevent fatigue.
notes.explanation: Avoid flying without a full night’s rest, after excessive hours, or after an exhausting day.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 47

notes.front: Does diet, rest and sleep relieve chronic fatigue?
notes.back: No; it usually needs treatment by a physician.
notes.explanation: Chronic fatigue usually has psychological roots, sometimes an underlying disease.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 47

notes.front: What is “timing disruption” in skill fatigue?
notes.back: Doing a task seemingly as usual, but with each component’s timing slightly off, so the whole is less smooth.
notes.explanation: The other effect is disruption of the perceptual field.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 46

notes.front: What is “disruption of the perceptual field” in skill fatigue?
notes.back: Focusing on the centre of vision and neglecting the periphery, with less accurate, less smooth control movements.
notes.explanation: The other effect is timing disruption.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 47

notes.front: What is the first noticeable effect of dehydration?
notes.back: Fatigue.
notes.explanation: If fluid is not replaced it progresses to dizziness, weakness, nausea, tingling, cramps and extreme thirst.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 47

notes.front: How much water does the study guide suggest drinking to help prevent dehydration?
notes.back: Two to four quarts every 24 hours.
notes.explanation: It is only a guide, because each person is physiologically different.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 47

notes.front: Which drinks promote dehydration?
notes.back: Diuretic drinks: coffee, tea, alcohol and caffeinated soft drinks.
notes.explanation: Other causes are hot temperatures, wind and humidity.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 47

notes.front: At about what deficit do most people become thirsty?
notes.back: About 1.5 quarts, or 2 percent of body weight.
notes.explanation: The thirst mechanism arrives too late and is easily turned off, so drink before you feel thirsty.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 47

notes.front: In severe heat stress, how much should a person drink to help prevent heatstroke?
notes.back: One quart per hour (one pint per hour for moderate heat stress).
notes.explanation: Carry ample water and drink at frequent intervals, thirsty or not.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 48

notes.front: How may the onset of heatstroke be recognised?
notes.back: By the symptoms of dehydration, but sometimes only upon complete collapse.
notes.explanation: That is why prevention (frequent drinking) matters more than waiting for symptoms.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 48

notes.front: In a visual scan, how wide an area should each stop cover?
notes.back: About 30°.
notes.explanation: Scan left to right or right to left, starting at the greatest distance and moving inward.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 50

notes.front: How long should each stop in a visual scan last at most?
notes.back: 2 to 3 seconds.
notes.explanation: The length depends on the detail needed, but no stop should exceed that.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 50

notes.front: By how much should each scan stop overlap the previous one?
notes.explanation: Overlap makes sure no strip of sky is skipped between stops.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 50

notes.front: Once fully dark-adapted, how much more sensitive to light are rods than cones?
notes.back: About 10,000 times.
notes.explanation: That makes rods the primary receptors for night vision.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Night Blind Spot”, p. 17-22

notes.front: To see an object clearly at night, how far off centre should a pilot look?
notes.back: 5° to 10° off centre.
notes.explanation: That puts the image on the rods, outside the night blind spot.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Night Blind Spot”, p. 17-22

notes.front: With off-centre viewing at night, why should you not hold your gaze on one spot for more than 2 to 3 seconds?
notes.back: The image fades as the rods reach equilibrium; shift to another off-centre point.
notes.explanation: Peripheral vision keeps the object in view as the eyes move between off-centre points.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Scanning Techniques”, p. 17-23

notes.front: About how long do the rods take to adapt fully to darkness?
notes.back: About 30 minutes.
notes.explanation: Cones adapt quickly; rods take much longer.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Dark Adaptation”, p. 17-23

notes.front: What does a bright light do to night adaptation?
notes.back: It can completely destroy it, so the adaptation process must start again.
notes.explanation: Rods take much longer than cones to adapt, so recovery is slow.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Dark Adaptation”, p. 17-23

notes.front: What does the PHAK suggest wearing in bright sunlight before a night flight?
notes.back: Neutral density (N-15) sunglasses or equivalent filter lenses.
notes.explanation: They increase the rate of dark adaptation and improve night sensitivity.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Sunglasses”, p. 17-24

notes.front: Which light period does the PHAK call the most dangerous for viewing?
notes.back: Mesopic vision: dawn, dusk and full moonlight, when rods and cones share the work.
notes.explanation: As cone sensitivity falls, use off-centre vision and proper scanning to detect objects.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Mesopic Vision”, p. 17-21

notes.front: At low light (scotopic vision), about what does visual acuity fall to?
notes.back: 20/200 or less, with colour lost.
notes.explanation: In very low light you see only objects as large as the big “E” on an eye chart from 20 feet, and no colour.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Scotopic Vision”, p. 17-21

notes.front: Besides sharpness and colour, what else may be lost at night?
notes.back: Depth perception and judgement of size.
notes.explanation: This makes judging the distance of an aircraft’s light harder at night.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Night Blind Spot”, p. 17-23

notes.front: Without supplemental oxygen, above what pressure altitude does night vision decline measurably?
notes.back: 4,000 feet.
notes.explanation: Night vision depends on the rods, which lose sensitivity with lack of oxygen.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Oxygen Supply”, p. 17-24

notes.front: When does apparent movement of a stared-at light (autokinesis) begin?
notes.back: In about 8 to 10 seconds.
notes.explanation: Do not stare at a light for more than 10 seconds.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Autokinesis”, p. 17-26

notes.front: What is the most important way to prevent autokinesis?
notes.back: Visual scanning, rather than fixating on a single light.
notes.explanation: Increasing the number of lights or varying their intensity also helps.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Autokinesis”, p. 17-26

notes.front: Flying towards a shoreline at night, how can a false horizon arise?
notes.back: The dark water makes shoreline lights look like stars in the sky.
notes.explanation: Confusing bright stars and city lights can also create a false horizon.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “False Horizon”, p. 17-26

notes.front: The PHAK’s self-imposed stressors that can limit night vision are {{c1::drugs}}, exhaustion, poor physical conditioning, alcohol, tobacco and hypoglycemia and nutritional deficiency.
notes.explanation: Each is under the pilot’s own control, so each can be avoided before a night flight.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Self-Imposed Stress”, p. 17-25

notes.front: The PHAK’s self-imposed stressors that can limit night vision are drugs, {{c1::exhaustion}}, poor physical conditioning, alcohol, tobacco and hypoglycemia and nutritional deficiency.
notes.explanation: Each is under the pilot’s own control, so each can be avoided before a night flight.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Self-Imposed Stress”, p. 17-25

notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Self-Imposed Stress”, p. 17-25

notes.front: The PHAK’s self-imposed stressors that can limit night vision are drugs, exhaustion, poor physical conditioning, alcohol, tobacco and {{c1::hypoglycemia (low blood sugar from missed meals) and nutritional deficiency}}.
notes.explanation: Each is under the pilot’s own control, so each can be avoided before a night flight.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Self-Imposed Stress”, p. 17-25

notes.front: Of all self-imposed stressors, which most decreases visual sensitivity at night?
notes.back: Cigarette smoking.
notes.explanation: Smokers lose about 20 percent of their night vision at sea level.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Tobacco”, p. 17-25

notes.front: Which vitamin deficiency may impair night vision?
notes.back: Vitamin A.
notes.explanation: Plenty of vitamin A does not improve night vision, but a lack of it impairs it.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Hypoglycemia and Nutritional Deficiency”, p. 17-25

notes.front: After a near miss with a helicopter, your visual observer is breathing fast and reports tingling fingers and dizziness. What is likely happening, and what helps?
notes.back: Hyperventilation; slow the breathing, breathe into a paper bag, or talk aloud.
notes.choices:
A) Hyperventilation
B) Heatstroke
C) Chronic fatigue
notes.choicesExplained: B: heatstroke is an inability to control body temperature; nothing here points to heat. C: chronic fatigue builds over a long period and is not triggered by a single fright.
notes.explanation: Stress-driven fast breathing lowers carbon dioxide and causes these symptoms.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 46

notes.front: After four hours in summer sun drinking only coffee, you have a headache, feel sleepy and have cramps. Which condition is this?
notes.back: Dehydration.
notes.explanation: Heat, wind and diuretic drinks such as coffee cause it; headache, fatigue, cramps, sleepiness and dizziness are signs.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 47

notes.front: You face a full day of hot-weather mapping flights. How should you guard against heatstroke?
notes.back: Carry ample water and drink at frequent intervals, whether thirsty or not.
notes.explanation: Heatstroke may only show on collapse, so prevention matters.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 48

notes.front: Your doctor prescribes a new medicine this morning. You have a job tomorrow morning. May you fly it?
notes.back: Not advised: wait at least 48 hours after the first dose to check for side effects.
notes.explanation: Tomorrow morning is less than 48 hours after the first dose.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 49

notes.front: You have a cold and took an antihistamine last night. You feel a bit drowsy. What should you do about today’s flight?
notes.back: Do not fly: antihistamines can cause drowsiness and cognitive deficits, and drowsiness is present.
notes.explanation: A drug that affects your faculties contrary to safety rules you out.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 48

notes.front: You drank heavily at a party that ended 10 hours ago and have a hangover. Is it safe to fly because 8 hours have passed?
notes.back: No; with a hangover you are still under the influence, and alcohol can remain for over 16 hours.
notes.explanation: Meeting the 8-hour rule does not make you fit; be more conservative than the regulations.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 49

notes.front: After a 16-hour working day, a client asks you to fly one more quick job. You feel “fine”. What should you do?
notes.back: Decline; no training or experience overcomes fatigue, and only adequate rest prevents it.
notes.explanation: Acute fatigue rules out operating a small UA.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 47

notes.front: For months you have had severe money and family worries, and your concentration at work has collapsed. Should you keep flying?
notes.back: No; this sounds like chronic stress: stop flying and see a doctor.
notes.explanation: Chronic stress exceeds the ability to cope and performance falls sharply.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 46

notes.front: A dog runs under your landing aircraft and your heart races. Is this acute or chronic stress?
notes.back: Acute stress: an immediate threat triggering “fight or flight”.
notes.explanation: Chronic stress is long-term and cumulative.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 46

notes.front: You are scanning the sky for traffic around your job site. What does one correct scan stop look like?
notes.back: A block about 30° wide, looked at for no more than 2–3 seconds, overlapping the last by 10°.
notes.explanation: Work left to right or right to left, from far to near.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 50

notes.front: At night your drone’s light fades whenever you look straight at it. What should you do?
notes.back: Look 5° to 10° off centre, moving your gaze every 2–3 seconds.
notes.explanation: The centre of vision has a night blind spot; the rods off centre see dim light better.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Night Blind Spot”, p. 17-22

notes.front: You arrive at a dark site straight from a brightly lit office for a night flight. What should you allow for?
notes.back: About 30 minutes for full dark adaptation, and avoid bright lights meanwhile.
notes.explanation: Rods adapt slowly, and bright light resets the process.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Dark Adaptation”, p. 17-23

notes.front: During a night flight you turn your phone to full brightness to read a checklist. What have you probably done to your night vision?
notes.back: Destroyed your dark adaptation; use a dim light instead.
notes.explanation: Bright light can completely destroy night adaptation, and it then takes time to recover.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Dark Adaptation”, p. 17-23

notes.front: At night, you stare for 15 seconds at your hovering drone’s single light and it seems to drift, though telemetry shows it is still. Which illusion is this?
notes.back: Autokinesis.
notes.choices:
A) Autokinesis
B) False horizon
C) Night blind spot
notes.choicesExplained: B: a false horizon is mistaking a feature for the horizon, not apparent movement of a light. C: the blind spot makes a light disappear when looked at directly, not drift.
notes.explanation: Staring at a single light against darkness makes it appear to move; keep scanning.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Autokinesis”, p. 17-26

notes.front: Flying at night near a lake, you misjudge your aircraft’s attitude because lights along the far shore blend with the stars. Which illusion is this?
notes.back: False horizon.
notes.explanation: Shore lights beyond dark water can be mistaken for stars, hiding the true horizon.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “False Horizon”, p. 17-26

notes.front: You fly during evening civil twilight. According to the PHAK, why is this a demanding time to see?
notes.back: It is mesopic vision, the most dangerous viewing period; use off-centre vision and proper scanning.
notes.explanation: As cone sensitivity decreases, off-centre vision and scanning help detect objects.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Mesopic Vision”, p. 17-21

notes.front: A remote pilot smokes several cigarettes before a night job. What is the effect on night vision?
notes.back: A marked loss: smokers lose about 20 percent of night vision capability at sea level.
notes.explanation: Carbon monoxide from smoke reduces oxygen carried in the blood.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Tobacco”, p. 17-25

notes.front: At night you find it hard to tell how far away your drone is, though you can see its light clearly. Which night-vision limitation explains this?
notes.back: Loss of depth perception (and judgement of size) at night.
notes.explanation: Along with sharpness and colour, depth perception and size judgement may be lost at night.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Night Blind Spot”, p. 17-23

notes.front: Your visual observer says he is still “a bit drunk” from last night. Whose responsibility is it that he does not take part?
notes.back: Yours, as remote PIC.
notes.explanation: The remote PIC must ensure no crew member participates while impaired.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 45

notes.front: You have epilepsy, currently well controlled. Who must decide whether you can fly safely today?
notes.back: You do, as remote PIC: you must determine the condition is under control and you can operate safely.
notes.explanation: Epilepsy is the study guide’s example of a condition that may create a risk.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 45

notes.front: You had one glass of wine 7 hours ago and feel completely normal. May you act as a crew member now?
notes.back: No; at least 8 hours must pass after drinking, whatever your blood alcohol level.
notes.explanation: A pilot cannot fly sooner than 8 hours after drinking even if well below 0.04 percent.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 50

notes.front: You skipped lunch and dinner before a night inspection flight. Which self-imposed stressor is this, and what can it cause?
notes.back: Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar), which can distract you and shorten your attention span.
notes.explanation: Missing or postponing meals impairs night flight performance.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Hypoglycemia and Nutritional Deficiency”, p. 17-25

notes.front: Late in a long filming session your stick inputs become jerky and you notice only the centre of the screen. Which type of fatigue does this suggest?
notes.back: Skill fatigue.
notes.explanation: Its two effects are timing disruption and disruption of the perceptual field.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 46

notes.front: Acute versus chronic fatigue: which is relieved by rest and sleep?
notes.back: Acute fatigue; chronic fatigue is not relieved by rest and usually needs a physician.
notes.explanation: Acute follows strenuous effort or lost sleep; chronic extends over a long period.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 47

notes.front: Dehydration versus heatstroke: which is a failure to control body temperature?
notes.back: Heatstroke; dehydration is a critical loss of water.
notes.explanation: Heatstroke may begin with dehydration symptoms, or show only as collapse.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 9, p. 48

notes.front: Rods versus cones: which give colour and fine detail?
notes.back: Cones; rods see in dim light and detect movement but not colour.
notes.explanation: Cones cluster at the centre of vision, rods towards the periphery.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Vision in Flight”, p. 17-20

notes.front: Autokinesis versus false horizon: which makes a still light seem to move?
notes.back: Autokinesis; a false horizon makes you misjudge where the horizon is.
notes.explanation: Both fool the eyes; both are common at night.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C (2023), ch. 17, “Night Vision Illusions”, p. 17-26
